record.original_question: Characterize which sequences produce the paper's 'spiral' type of associated 4-regular graph. In particular, make precise the heuristic that spiral graphs arise from consecutive blocks of increasing subsequences, and determine how far the model a(n,k)=exp(k(f(n)-f(k))) captures the full phenomenon after reading the triangular array by rows and removing duplicates.

evidence.quote: We do not have a clear characterization but it does seem like such sequences arises from having consecutive segments of increasing subsequences.
This construction is inspired by binomial coefficient asymptotics, the full extent of the phenomenon is not currently understood.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Construction. Given a finite list of n distinct real numbers x_1, x_2, ..., x_n (an "ordered sequence"), associate to it a 4-regular graph G = (V, E) on n vertices labeled 1, ..., n as follows: connect vertex i (for 2 ≤ i ≤ n−1) to its two left neighbors and two right neighbors in the list when ranked by value, in the natural cyclic manner used to build the so-called "horizontal/vertical-visibility-style" 4-regular graph; equivalently, for each index i let p(i) and q(i) be the indices of the largest j < i with x_j < x_i and with x_j > x_i (respectively), and let r(i), s(i) be the analogous indices on the right side, and connect i to {p(i), q(i), r(i), s(i)} (with boundary conventions making the graph 4-regular).

Empirically, certain input sequences produce drawings of G that look like a "spiral": a long curve that winds around itself in a regular pattern. One source of such examples comes from triangular arrays: given a function a(n,k) defined for 1 ≤ k ≤ n, list the values a(1,1), a(2,1), a(2,2), a(3,1), a(3,2), a(3,3), ... by rows, then delete duplicates while preserving order, and feed the resulting sequence into the construction. In particular, the model a(n,k) = exp(k (f(n) − f(k))) for various functions f produces spiral graphs.

Problem. 
(a) Give a precise characterization of which input sequences (x_1, ..., x_n) give rise to a spiral 4-regular graph under this construction.
(b) In particular, formalize and prove (or refute) the heuristic that spiral graphs arise exactly from sequences that decompose into consecutive blocks of increasing subsequences (specifying the block-length growth required).
(c) Determine the full class of triangular arrays a(n,k) whose row-by-row, duplicate-removed reading produces a spiral graph, and decide to what extent this class is captured by the family a(n,k) = exp(k (f(n) − f(k))) as f ranges over a natural class of functions.
artifact.status_search_result: The construction and the spiral phenomenon are introduced in a problem list on graphs from sequences, where the authors explicitly state they do not have a clear characterization and that the full extent of the phenomenon is not currently understood. No subsequent work resolving the characterization was found.

status_evidence.title: Finding Structure in Sequences of Real Numbers via Graph Theory: a Problem List
status_evidence.snippet: Spirals are frequently encountered; such sequences appear to arise from having consecutive segments of increasing subsequences. The full extent of the phenomenon is not currently understood.
status_evidence.claim: Authors explicitly state the spiral characterization is open.
